meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a misattribution. Seneca really wrote it, in Letter 101 of the Moral Letters to Lucilius (c. AD 65), Gummere's Loeb translation.

answer.sourceLine: From Seneca’s Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 101 (“On the Futility of Planning Ahead”), §10, written c. AD 65. The familiar English is Richard M. Gummere’s Loeb translation of the Latin ‘Ideo propera, Lucili mi, vivere, et singulos dies singulas vitas puta.’

source.excerpt: … when a soundly-balanced mind knows that a day differs not a whit from eternity — then the soul looks forth from lofty heights and laughs heartily to itself… Therefore, my dear Lucilius, begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.
trail: The English wording is Richard M. Gummere’s Loeb translation, printed in Seneca’s Letter 101, §10 ↗.
The underlying Latin, ‘Ideo propera, Lucili mi, vivere, et singulos dies singulas vitas puta,’ appears in the standard Latin edition ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Letter CI, ‘On the Futility of Planning Ahead.’
source.excerptNote: The maxim caps Seneca’s argument that anxious planning steals the present: only someone unhappy with today frets about tomorrow.
source.rightsNote: The Latin is ancient and Gummere’s English translation (Loeb, 1917–25) is out of U.S. copyright — both are public domain.

author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (“Seneca the Younger”) was a Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist, and statesman who served as tutor and later adviser to the emperor Nero. His Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium — 124 letters on Stoic ethics and everyday living — rank among the most widely read works of ancient philosophy. Ordered by Nero to take his own life in AD 65, he died much as he had counselled others to live.

context.heading: Living each day as a whole life
lead: Letter 101 is Seneca’s meditation on the futility of planning too far ahead. He argues that only a person dissatisfied with the present frets over the future — and that a well-ordered mind treats a single day as no different from eternity.
The closing maxim distills that Stoic outlook: do not postpone living, and let each day stand complete, so that whenever death comes it finds a life already finished rather than merely interrupted.
context.pull: “A day differs not a whit from eternity.”
